cues.text:
OpenRTB carries bid requests and
responses.

ARTF, the Agentic Real Time Framework,
lets a host call specialist
services during the auction.

Let's see how their proposals become
changes buyers see.
The exchange is our host.

The agent is a specialist service inside
its infrastructure.
Here it returns fixed proposals.

The envelope wraps OpenRTB so the host can
request changes.

This call id is separate from the auction
id.

Matching it ties the answer to the right
call.

The time budget is one hundred fifty
milliseconds; a late answer
can miss the auction.
Intents name the jobs this host offers.
They limit what the agent can change.

Here that's segments, deals, floors, and
metrics.
Shading waits until there's a bid.

A mutation is a proposed change, with an
operation, target, and payload.
Here it adds audience segments.

Those labels can affect which campaigns
consider this impression.
The host chooses whether to apply it.

This floor change raises the premium
deal's minimum price from twelve dollars

to fourteen fifty per thousand
impressions.
That changes which bids qualify.

A higher floor can also leave the
impression without an eligible bid.

Content id wasn't offered here, so it's
skipped.

The DSP, the buyer's platform, still
receives four accepted changes.

Independent acceptance lets the host keep
useful work while enforcing its own rules.
This answer names the wrong call.

The host rejects the response before
applying any changes.

The original auction stays unchanged, and
nothing new reaches the buyer.

A usable proposal can't bypass that
identity check.
Deal margin shows an integration gap.

This host has no standard OpenRTB field
for it.

An intent needs an agreed mapping, or the
host cannot apply the proposal.
Here, viewability is the word high.
ARTF's typed metric requires a number.

Our HTTP JSON fixture introduces this
fault.

The resulting request gives the buyer a
value it cannot reliably use.

The mutation was applied, but the request
it produced is invalid.

That's why we check the assembled OpenRTB
too.

The host stops this error here, before a
buyer has to handle it.
RTBlint performs these checks in our demo.
ARTF provides the shared interface.
The host supplies the business rules.

That allows specialists to integrate
through a common contract while the
platform controls the auction.

In this separate bid response example,
eighteen forty becomes twelve eighty eight
for the same creative.

Shading changes the price competing in the
auction.

The exchange still decides whether the bid
qualifies.
OpenRTB carries the auction data.

ARTF gives specialists a common way to
propose changes, with the host in control.

Next, we'll coordinate several agents
around one auction.
